title: Are they just delegating? Cross-Sample Predictions on University Students' & Teachers' Use of AI.
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students and university teachers in higher education use generative AI, and whether they can accurately predict each other’s AI use. The authors focus on two dimensions of use: how frequently AI is used for academic tasks and how much those tasks are delegated to AI. The broader problem motivating the study is that inaccurate beliefs about the other group’s AI use may undermine trust between teachers and students, which the authors argue is important for effective teaching, learning, and assessment.

The study uses two online surveys administered in Germany, one for university teachers and one for university students. Participants reported their own AI use and AI delegation across academic tasks, and they also made incentivized predictions about the other group’s AI use. Analyses focused on six overlapping tasks relevant to both groups: information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, and visualizing. The approach is not an intervention in the experimental sense; rather, it is an observational survey design comparing self-reports and cross-sample predictions.

The population consisted of 113 university teachers and 123 university students in the abstract, though the methods section reports final analyzed samples of 123 teachers and 113 students from German universities across a range of disciplines, with some students recruited through Prolific after initial recruitment fell short. This places the study in a higher education context with students and educators as the main user groups. Because the paper concerns university participants rather than K-12, the relevant populations are undergraduate and graduate/doctoral students, along with adult educators.

The main findings are that students reported using AI more often and delegating more academic work to AI than teachers overall, although teachers reported higher AI use for translation tasks. Both groups substantially overestimated the other group’s AI use and delegation. Teachers tended to assume students used AI very frequently and delegated heavily, while students assumed teachers used AI at levels similar to themselves. The authors conclude that this perception gap may hinder trust and collaboration in higher education and argue for more open dialogue, transparency, and policy guidance around AI use in academic contexts.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools used for academic tasks in higher education, discussed collectively rather than as a specific product.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed university teachers and students about self-reported frequency of AI use and degree of delegation across six academic tasks (information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, visualizing), and about their predictions of the other group's AI use.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported using generative AI more frequently than teachers across academic tasks overall, with a small but significant main effect of group (b = -0.35, SE = 0.09, p < .001, d = 0.36). The largest differences favored students for information research (b = -0.73, SE = 0.15, p < .001, d = 0.75), programming (b = -0.61, SE = 0.15, p < .001, d = 0.63), literature research (b = -0.50, SE = 0.15, p = .001, d = 0.51), and text work (b = -0.48, SE = 0.15, p = .0009, d = 0.50), while teachers reported higher AI use for translation tasks (b = 0.36, SE = 0.15, p = .013, d = 0.37). The analyzed samples were teachers (N = 113) and students (N = 123) as stated in the abstract.
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use across six academic tasks on a 5-point scale
findings.effect_size: d = 0.36 overall; task-specific d values from 0.14 to 0.75

findings.finding_summary: Students reported delegating academic tasks to generative AI to a greater extent than teachers overall, with a medium-sized significant main effect (b = -15.72, SE = 2.46, p < .001, d = 0.66). The largest differences favored students for information research (b = -24.09, SE = 3.74, p < .001, d = 1.02), writing (b = -19.25, SE = 3.74, p < .001, d = 0.81), literature research (b = -18.06, SE = 3.75, p < .001, d = 0.76), and programming (b = -17.78, SE = 3.80, p < .001, d = 0.75); translation was not significant (b = -5.04, SE = 3.75, p = .180, d = 0.21). The analyzed samples were teachers (N = 113) and students (N = 123) as stated in the abstract.
findings.measure: Self-reported degree of AI delegation across six academic tasks on a 0-100 scale
findings.effect_size: d = 0.66 overall; task-specific d values from 0.21 to 1.02

findings.finding_summary: Both groups significantly overestimated the other group's frequency of AI use by 1.02 points on average, indicating large prediction inaccuracy (b = 1.02, SE = 0.02, p < .001, d = 1.75). Students were only slightly more accurate than teachers in one analysis (b = -0.093, SE = 0.05, t(234) = -2.05, p = .042, d = 0.16), but the authors note this effect disappeared with the alternative student sample.
findings.measure: Prediction accuracy for frequency of AI use, calculated as absolute difference between predicted and actual group mean

findings.finding_summary: Both groups significantly overestimated the other group's degree of AI delegation by 25.89 points on average, reflecting very large inaccuracy (b = 25.89, SE = 0.69, p < .001, d = 2.08). There was no significant difference between teachers and students in prediction accuracy for delegation (b = -2.43, SE = 1.38, t(233.98) = -1.76, p = .079, d = 0.20).
findings.measure: Prediction accuracy for degree of AI delegation, calculated as absolute difference between predicted and actual group mean

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical survey study with cross-sample prediction analyses, but it relies on self-reports rather than experimental or quasi-experimental causal designs. The methodology is clear and preregistered, yet the evidence is correlational/descriptive rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are medium to very large for several outcomes, including delegation differences (d = 0.66 overall) and prediction inaccuracies (d = 1.75 and d = 2.08). Although the outcomes are perceptual and behavioral self-reports rather than direct learning gains, the magnitude of reported effects is substantial.
